To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the best designs for estimating the effective dose are those that have the highest power for detecting the effective dose.

(1) the design with the highest precision is not always the most desirable, (2) the design that maximizes precision is not the same as the design that minimizes the variance of the estimate of the effective dose, (3) the design that minimises the variance of the estimated effective dose is not the same design that minimises bias, and (4) the design that gives the smallest variance of the estimate is not always the same design that gives the minimum bias.
the optimal design for estimating an effective dose is the design with the largest value for the information matrix, which can be obtained by using the method described above.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of designing experiments to estimate effective doses.
developing methods of estimating effective doses when there is some prior information on the dose‐relationship, but not enough to permit a precise estimate of the effective dose.
the design of experiments for estimating effective doses when there is some information available on the dose response relationship.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, when the dose‐response curve is known to be linear, a design with a single dose level at the estimated effective dose is optimal.
the method of maximum likelihood is to be preferred, and that it is to be preferred over the method of least squares.
the experimental design should consist of a number of doses, with the highest dose chosen so that it is expected that at least 20% of the animals will show a response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the designs chosen for estimating effective doses are not necessarily the best possible designs for estimating other parameters in the dose‐relationship.
a large number of dose levels is required when the dose‐response function is not linear and when the dose‐effect is large.

the optimal design for the estimation of the effective dose is a design with the largest number of dose points, and with these points chosen to have the same spacing as the dose points in the design that maximizes the information about the dose‐response curve.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it is possible to choose an experimental design which will give an unbiased estimate of the effective dose with a minimum variance, even when very little information on the dose‐ response relationship is available prior to experimentation.

, when there is little prior information on the dose‐effect relationship, a design that is based on a linear approximation to the dose‐response curve is likely to provide the most information about the effective dose.
a linear approximation to the dose‐response curve is adequate in the estimation of effective doses.
